steps.action:
# The Last Light

Every evening at dusk, Marion climbed the 112 steps.

She had counted them the first week she took the job, back when her knees were younger and her husband was still alive. Now she counted them out of habit, the way some people count their breaths.

The lighthouse sat on a finger of rock off the Maine coast, and Marion had kept it for thirty-one years. The Coast Guard had offered to automate it twice. Both times she'd declined, though she couldn't fully explain why, even to herself.

On a Tuesday in November, a nor'easter came in hard and fast. The radio crackled warnings. Marion lit the lamp early, watched it begin its slow rotation, and stood at the glass with her coffee growing cold in her hands.

Around midnight, she saw the fishing boat.

It was running too close to the rocks — she could tell by the way it moved, uncertain, like something frightened. She grabbed the radio and called in the position. Then she did the only other thing she could do.

She kept the light turning.

Twenty minutes later the boat corrected course. She watched it find the deep water channel and disappear into the dark. She never learned the name of the vessel or who was aboard.

She washed her cup, turned off the kitchen light, and climbed back up the 112 steps to make sure the lamp was still burning.

It was. It always was.

That was the whole job, really. Not heroics. Just the steady, faithful refusal to go dark.
